Well animated, and so far well balanced. The feature to build your deck is yet to be released due to early access, but it doesn't get in the way of having fun. The levels are short but challenging, the meta improvements and unlocks are varied, plentiful, and diverse. I will say that the meta improvements (perma unlocks for future runs) are perhaps the least interesting part of the game, being "add 1% to this" or "+2 defence". So I'd like to see that changed to be more interesting and meaningful. All said, even early on I can tell this is already one worth playing and one worth watching.

The game has a unique atmosphere & many interesting mechanics that evolve the genre, enjoyable gameplay, but the build is still very rough atm. This includes the unintuitive UI/UX, a poor tutorial, and terrible metaprogression like +1% health regeneration. Metaprogress should be about unlocking and buying new cards, not this outdated grinding mechanic. In the first run, 80% of the gameplay time is spent reading encounters menus, not the gameplay itself, and I personally think that's too much. Fans of the original game will be pleased. Still it's definitely not a refund.

I bought Hand of Fate: Hordes on launch day and went in completely blind. After my first 90 minutes, I genuinely did not want to stop playing. The dark fantasy art style, the colour palette, the music, and especially the Dealer’s narration immediately pulled me in. The combat can turn from simple to complete chaos very quickly, but every upgrade makes a difference and you can feel the build changing as the run continues. I usually prefer turn-based games, so the faster pace and keyboard movement were a real challenge for me. I made plenty of wrong moves, died during the tutorial, and later found myself running through a horde with only one HP left — but I was having fun the entire time. Based on my first 90 minutes, the game already feels full of possibilities. Different heroes, cards, goals, and strategies should make every run feel different. It is still Early Access, so I need more time before judging the long-term content and balance, but as a first impression, this was extremely strong. Recommended — and definitely not my last run.

《命运之手：人各有命》是由Spitfire Interactive开发，充满掷骰子RNG乐趣的一款弹幕射击肉鸽游戏。 [h3]白白点赞：[/h3] 1.作为外传与系列前作画风统一，原汁原味。 2.关卡特色强，每关都有属于自己的场景元素和任务，首通新鲜感爆棚。 3.首发236张卡牌，发牌人派牌决定行进路线，祝福诅咒和敌人多寡，形式新颖。 4.骰子、卡背、英雄外观支持换肤。 5.敌人随时间不断增强，击败Boss开启撤离倒计时，紧迫感十足。 6.主创团队解散后重整旗鼓，韧性可嘉！ [h3]白白开喷：[/h3] 1.“WASD”操控技能指向存在偏差，近战系较突出。 2.局内升级奖励重抽成本高，吃经济，很难爽D。 3.动效稍显笨拙。 4.目前不支持倍速。 [h3]新手攻略：[/h3] 1.前期优先获取碎片奖励，提升局外属性。 2.事件区域临近的时候，建议占住重叠部分，事半功倍。 3.新手推关建议主用战士，整整5点护甲的被动，叠加局外属性，容错拉满。

Having a blast with this so far and I'm really excited to see where Early Access takes it. The art style and soundtrack are fantastic, the moment-to-moment gameplay feels great, and there is already tons of replay value. Especially as a returning Hand of Fate player, the cards and encounter events are beautifully designed. Plus, the Dealer's voice acting and commentary are brilliant as always and add so much atmosphere. As for early feedback, I feel like the Warrior takes damage a bit too fast right now and could use a slight tuning in terms of survivability. Also, the stat upgrades (like +x%) feel a little uninspired, so having more unique or impactful choices would make runs even more exciting. Overall, a super solid foundation and definitely worth playing. Looking forward to future updates!

Hand of Fate: Hordes demonstrates that the Hand of Fate franchise still has plenty of life left in it, even as it ventures into a genre far removed from its card-table origins. Developed by Spitfire Interactive and published by Spicy Koala, the game transforms the series into a roguelite horde survival experience while preserving many of the elements that made the original titles memorable. Set within the mysterious Shadow Vaults beyond the infamous 13th Gate, players once again find themselves under the watchful eye of the Dealer, whose unmistakable voice and ominous presence provide a constant reminder that every victory comes at a price. Rather than abandoning the franchise's identity, Hand of Fate: Hordes cleverly integrates its signature card mechanics into the fast-paced gameplay loop. Players select from a roster of heroes that range from melee-focused fighters to spellcasters and agile tricksters, each bringing a different approach to combat. The deckbuilding component remains central to progression, allowing players to influence the types of encounters, blessings, equipment, and modifiers they will encounter during a run. This system creates an additional layer of strategy rarely seen in the increasingly crowded bullet heaven genre, giving players meaningful decisions both before entering battle and during their attempts to survive increasingly overwhelming enemy waves. The combat itself is satisfying and chaotic in equal measure. Battles quickly escalate into screen-filling encounters where positioning, build choices, and timely upgrades become essential. What distinguishes Hand of Fate: Hordes from many of its contemporaries is its willingness to interrupt the action with familiar franchise staples, including card draws, chance-based events, and dice rolls. These moments reinforce the feeling that the Dealer is orchestrating every challenge, ensuring that each run feels less like a simple survival exercise and more like a chapter in an ongoing dark fantasy campaign. Unlockable blessings, weapon rarities, and permanent progression systems provide additional incentives to continue experimenting with different combinations. Narratively, the game benefits greatly from its presentation. Anthony Skordi's performance as the Dealer remains one of the strongest aspects of the entire franchise, bringing an unsettling charisma to every interaction. His narration lends weight to the proceedings and elevates the atmosphere considerably. Even players unfamiliar with the previous Hand of Fate entries can appreciate the game's world-building, while returning fans will undoubtedly enjoy revisiting one of indie gaming's most distinctive antagonists. The setting itself is suitably grim, with environments that emphasize mystery and danger without sacrificing gameplay readability during the more intense encounters. From a visual standpoint, Hand of Fate: Hordes strikes a pleasing balance between style and functionality. Its dark fantasy aesthetic complements the source material, and the various magical effects, enemy designs, and environments contribute to an immersive experience. The soundtrack supports the mood effectively, while the overall presentation demonstrates a level of polish that is impressive for an Early Access title. Performance is generally stable, and the game's interface does a commendable job of communicating large amounts of information without overwhelming the player during combat. As an Early Access release, however, there are limitations worth acknowledging. While the existing content offers a solid foundation, it is clear that the game is still in the process of realizing its full potential. The developers have outlined plans for additional heroes, bosses, quests, dungeons, and gameplay modes over the coming months, suggesting that the current version represents only the beginning of a larger experience. Fortunately, the core gameplay loop is already compelling enough to justify its present state, and the transparent development roadmap provides confidence that future updates will continue to expand and refine the experience. Hand of Fate: Hordes succeeds because it refuses to be a simple imitation of genre trends. Instead, it uses the established mechanics of horde survival games as a framework for delivering something uniquely tied to the Hand of Fate universe. Its blend of deckbuilding, roguelite progression, atmospheric storytelling, and satisfying combat creates an experience that feels both familiar and refreshingly distinct. While some players may prefer to wait for the game to leave Early Access, those willing to jump in now will find an inventive and entertaining title with a promising future ahead. Rating: 8/10

A fun addition to the Hand of Fate series. Same unlocking of cards and 4 Card Monte gameplay that has been a staple of this series, but now instead of the individual battles of the first 2 games, now each battle is played out in an obstacle filled battlefield in the form of a typical Survivor/Bullet Heaven game.

Unfortunately, it's no for me. I loved the narrative aspect of HoF and HoF:2, far less the combat aspect of those games. I was *very* interested in the new take for this new game. Here, I quite like the gameplay, but unfortunately I don't feel the constant interruptions to continue the HoF narration during the main game are a positive thing here: survivor games are all about in-the-moment adrenaline, not RPG-like narration. On the other hand, the out-of-combat part of this game is very empty: select the hero, select adventure, select +x%-style metaprogression. It feels like a wasted opportunity. I will keep an eye on this, I hope the direction of the game can still change during Early Access.
